title: Why definitions vary: whole essence vs the differentia from historical faith
source_text: XVI. Porro quod tam varie fidem definiunt Doctores Reformati, inde est quod nonnulli totam ejus essentiam describere nituntur, nempe, tam id quod habet commune cum fide, quam historicam vocant, quam id quod est illius proprium: alii vero solum id notare intendunt quo fides justificans ab historica differt. Praeterea alii fidem justificantem ex una proprietate, alii vero ex alia describunt; quae tamen non sunt inter se opponenda, sed componenda: cum tam horum, quam illorum Theologorum judicio, utramque proprietatem fides illa sibi vendicet; licet hujus, aut illius tantum expressam faciant in sua descriptione mentionem.
pass_a_gloss: Further, that the Reformed Doctors define faith so variously comes from this: that some strive to describe its whole essence — namely both what it has in common with that faith which they call historical, and what is proper to it — while others intend only to note that by which justifying faith differs from historical. Besides, some describe justifying faith from one property, others from another; which yet are not to be opposed to each other, but composed: since in the judgment of both these and those Theologians that faith claims both properties for itself; though they make express mention in their description of this one, or of that one, only.
pass_b_english: Varied definitions are not random conflict.
Some sketch the whole essence (shared with historical + what is proper).
Others mark only the differentia from historical faith.
One property or another in the wording — both belong; combine, don’t oppose.
